A large number of households in the UK went for the BBC Micro as the first PC for the family. A lot of my friends had them. But my parents chose to buy a Sinclair Spectrum 48k. It my first PC but not my introduction to gaming (had an Atari 2600 with a handful of games, including River Raid).

Fondest memories with the 48k was playing games for hours on on end like Way of the Exploding Fist, Beach Head, Spy Hunter, Head over Heels and Ghosts and Goblins. And then there were the woefully disappointing Arcade conversations of games like Outrun and Operation Wolf, which of course, fell painfully short of their original Arcade incarnations. At the time I couldn't comprehend why these games didn't look or play anything like the Arcade versions.

From the 48k, my family graduated to the Amiga 500 which was a revelation at the time. Most of friends had an Atari ST and the arguments that raged between us about which machine was superior would go on and on. Kind of similar to how young gamers whom own one or the other leading consoles of this generation, endlessly argue which is better. Nothing much changes when you think about it.

So yeah, 48k was my first introduction to PC gaming. But of course in the early 1980's, PC gaming was nothing like it is today. This year I turned forty years old and I don't see myself stopping playing video games on my system any time soon.
Wolfenstein 3d and Descent (damn I feel old). Never looked back after being able to use a mouse and keyboard vs a controller (except for Nintendo until after the N64, the last great console).

Wolfenstein 3D was the first game that made me want to get a newer computer (we had an IBM AT at my Mom's home), combined with Chuck Yeager's Air Combat, Doom, Ultima 7 (Part 1 especially), Blakestone, and a bunch of other games, consoles didn't interest me as much.

I was also quite fond of the Apple IIe and the C64 when I had a chance to use them.

I also like(d) the backwards compatibility and the ability to change games via mods.

I was introduced to PC gaming at the same time as our first NES. They felt kind of on the same level at that time, except the PC was more private and the games usually more comfortably paced. Moderately better looking. So it was a slightly better fit for me from the start. Add to that the PC having plenty of other capabilities for me to constantly learn about, feeding my early fascination with technology. The NES just... played games, and arcadey ones at that.

From then on, there was a torrent of awesome games on PC while every new console seemed to get further and further behind the PCs of its time. That's all, really.

I was also a big lover of multiplayer games and felt consoles only really did multiplayer well in fighting games, bullet hells, etc.—genres that didn't necessitate split-screen.
The fact that consoles just became the worst of aspects of PC with none of the major benefits. That was it for me. Switched permanently once and for all.
Duke Nukem 3D. As a young child this game was scary as f***. Keep in mind I was playing Putt Putt and Lego Island at the time.

That's what I started gaming on. Wolfenstein 3D, Quake, Doom, Marble Madness (On the Commodore Amiga), the list goes on. PC gaming is also responsible for my interest in computers which turned into a career. Thanks Wolfenstein!
